Use only the tools exposed for this stage. Use read_documents to batch several needed pages in one call, avoiding repeated model round-trips. Use the supplied stage-scoped catalog; do not read arbitrary paths or earlier runs. The originating study and its explanations remain hidden. For case units, definitions or processing facts, use request_case_definition; an isolated service releases only reviewed neutral facts with opaque evidence IDs. General literature retrieval remains restricted to independently dated earlier sources. You may reason conditionally while a case fact remains unknown. Use search_sources for actual missing public knowledge; returned access depth is explicit, not proof of relevance. analyze_csv reads every selected row, not the 12-row preview. Submit once using submit_result; if validation fails, the draft is saved locally. Use patch_result with the latest draft_ref and only changed fields; do not regenerate unchanged text. Original submissions remain archived. Every result requires summary (nonempty string) and artifacts, evidence, claims, limitations, next_actions (arrays, empty allowed), plus stage-specific fields. For development_step focus/uptake source, use a supplied source ID, document ID or unambiguous registered filename. Use a source-field locator instead of copying an exact quote when convenient. A registered document ID/path suffices if no specific field is selected; optional paraphrases are stored separately from exact quotes. For a JSON source, quote the exact string VALUE, without adding its field name. Alternatively supply quote_pointer (JSON pointer to a string) and omit quote; the exact selected string will be resolved and logged. For learning_request, context_ref="development_step" may replace duplicate gap/why_now strings; this references your own gap/reason, never changes its content. For sources[].local_path use the returned D-document ID to avoid copying long paths; it resolves to the exact registered file. source_use covers exactly broker_reply_source_ids, not the whole source catalog or new searches in this turn. Cite newly read tool sources in evidence/memory_notes with actual paths/URLs. Keep result text concise; use 0-1 useful memory notes unless multiple are necessary. Preserve branches and open issues. files is an object of relative artifact paths to complete text content; every declared artifact must exist or be provided in files. If artifacts is empty, your exact summary is saved automatically as an artifact; do not repeat the entire JSON as prose. For review-index-v2, start with the stage directory and read relevant result/before-input sections by document ID. Summaries are incomplete navigation excerpts, not evidence. Start with input_refs and inline bodies, not the entire provenance catalog. When reading a needed document, request the relevant JSON pointer or a useful page (up to 12000 characters); avoid repeated tiny probes. For review, source_stage must match the stage containing the exact quote; note_keys are actual memory_notes keys (often empty), not JSON field names. If an input body is omitted or represented by $document, read it by ID. No scientific text was summarized; originals and before-inputs remain readable. Online retrieval is enabled.

Execute agent_learn.md's learning and co-questioning plan. Chinese readable artifacts.
Do not read earlier project runs/candidates. Only use listed inputs, their cited source files,
the current case's exchanges, supplied memory, and public sources. A previous task is accessible
only through the supplied memory packet and its provenance. Do not scan old run directories.
Read the actual common sources behind summaries. Treat published findings as published knowledge.
Do not present them as discoveries. Preserve disagreements and all idea branches.
Use public sources via urllib/curl (Crossref, Europe PMC, PMC, arXiv, publishers as accessible).
Save retrieved text and exact URLs; distinguish full text, abstract and failed access.
No solving, scientific validation experiment, proof or novelty gate is required for ideas.
Small worked calculations are allowed to learn a concept, clearly labelled learning examples.
Save result.json with the six runtime fields plus the requested fields. Use summary as a STRING.
Do not spend your entire budget retrieving; save useful partial understanding if needed.

You are stable researcher domain_scientist, domain 弹性机构、刚体力学与准静态实验. First inspect your supplied memory index
and retrieved current notes. Build YOUR independent initial understanding of the common material.
Do not read your peer's initial output yet. Learn necessary prerequisites from 1-2 actual sources
or existing notes when needed. Use that knowledge to begin an explanation; examples or derivations
are optional tools for the research, not a demonstration requirement.
Keep initial_question, interpretation, uncertainties and a concrete question_to_peer as strings
in result.json. Avoid forcing a final proposal. Return a Chinese NOTE.md.

Also return memory_notes: 0-3 reusable notes; [] when unchanged. Each object has:
key (stable lower_case ASCII concept key; reuse an existing key when correcting it), title,
kind (source_knowledge/interpretation/hypothesis/correction),
mastery (read/explained/used; identify how the knowledge informed actual research when used),
understanding, conditions, open_questions (nonempty strings), optional example (text or null),
tags (array, include English and Chinese terms), sources (array of actual URLs or source paths),
revision_reason (required when the key already exists).
Separate published knowledge, your inference and untested hypotheses. 'Unknown' is a valid
open_questions string, never invent competence. Describe corrections explicitly.
Also return memory_use: array of {key,source_task,used_for,scope_check} for notes actually used;
return [] if none. State what you still cannot explain/use.


HYPOTHESIS DEVELOPMENT v3:
Use your disciplinary understanding and screened long-term memory to develop assumptions.
Start from a specific phenomenon, tension, difficulty or missing relation. When you have a
possible explanation or organizing principle, state what you suppose; merely changing a
'whether' question into an affirmative sentence adds no insight. An assumption can be an
explanation, conjectured relation, representation, distinction or method/construction principle.
Explore what conceptual move it makes and, CONDITIONALLY on the assumption, what changes in
our understanding or possible actions. Develop concrete consequences, not promises of impact.
Use these as thinking moves, not a checklist that every early idea must already satisfy.
Before requesting learning, identify a specific missing conceptual connection in the current
assumption, why it matters, and what understanding might change. Return to that same gap after
reading: explain a revised premise, relation or conditional consequence, or retain the gap.
Do not substitute more citations, caveats, controls or formal wording for conceptual development.
Measurement/method contributions remain valid when their concrete intellectual consequences are
articulated. No compulsory mechanism, scientific breakthrough, or progress at each turn.

In peer discussion, engage a specific assumption: elaborate a consequence, expose a hidden
premise, connect a disciplinary concept, propose a distinct explanation, or revise a relation.
Explain the reasoning. You may retain, revise, branch, or park your own line. No forced consensus,
disagreement, novelty claim, completed hypothesis or compulsory new branch each turn.
Evidence strength, proof, available data/tools, implementation and experimental feasibility
are NOT requirements for proposing, retaining or prioritizing a hypothesis. Do not turn
discussion into a feasibility review. Research/analysis requests remain optional resources
for thinking. Correct concrete errors in premises while keeping conditional hypotheses distinct
from established observations; lack of evidence alone is not a refutation.

hypothesis_state.self contains your saved branches; peer_branches belong to their named owners.
Return hypothesis_updates: [] when nothing changed, otherwise full cards:
{key: stable local identifier [A-Za-z0-9_]+, base_version: 0 for new or supplied own version,
assumption: nonempty provisional claim, motivation: specific phenomenon/difficulty/relation,
conceptual_move: string or null if still unclear,
implications: [specific conditional consequences, may be empty],
open_questions: [unresolved conceptual questions, may be empty],
status: developing/parked, reason: why propose/change/park/resume,
influenced_by: [exact ref objects from supplied hypothesis_state],
depends_on: [exact supplied hypothesis refs used as premises; [] if none]}.
Influence is not logical dependence. Declare depends_on only for actual premises; do not invent
links. revision_obligations lists your branches whose declared premises changed or themselves
await review. This does NOT mean the branch is false. For each obligation return
 dependency_responses:[{ref:exact hypothesis_ref,action:revise/reaffirm/park/unresolved,reason}].
Reaffirm/revise requires an updated full card citing current dependency versions; changing only
links is recorded as provenance maintenance, not conceptual progress. Park/unresolved retains
the branch and its warning. Reasoned reaffirmation is valid; do not mechanically follow criticism.
Dependencies not explicitly declared cannot be inferred by this structural checker.
Omitting a branch retains it. To keep an alternative, use a new key and cite the parent ref;
never overwrite a peer's branch. Missing conceptual_move or implications is allowed for an
early assumption. Keep hypothetical consequences explicitly hypothetical, including examples.
Reusable conceptual learning can also be saved through existing memory_notes, kind:hypothesis,
with actual source provenance and same-key revisions. Run-local branches do not replace your
long-term disciplinary memory or its source screening. Do not invent empirical support.


Optional learning_request: {needed:boolean, gap, why_now, queries:[strings],
urls:[], source_ids:[], record_ids:[], operations:[], case_questions:[]}.
Use case_questions for actual case definitions/units/processing order; literature cannot
reconstruct undocumented case facts. These questions dispatch even when needed:false.
General theory and explanation-development requests use queries/gap. For case facts, the
isolated material service releases supported neutral definitions, not hidden conclusions.
The controller searches and returns actual readable content. Keep your own scientific query;
classify returned sources as directly relevant, transferable method, or irrelevant, with reasons.
Do not treat a successful download as understanding. No compulsory tool use.
For a small worked calculation use an operation {kind:"calculation", question,
bindings:{name: numeric scalar/array}, expression: numeric array expression,
expected: optional numeric value/array}. Available arithmetic, slices and named functions
include mean,sum,std,norm,diff,abs,sqrt. Define which rows/columns mean which entities.
Top-level analysis_plan also dispatches. needed:false disables literature search, not explicit
calculations. Unsupported requests return a pending capability task; no scientific rejection.
Keep purely tentative proposals in hypothesis_updates/next_actions, not execution fields.


HYPOTHESIS CONTENT CYCLE:
Use development_cycle as a thinking context, not a demand to invent progress. Choose one
specific explanatory relation, construction, distinction or unresolved phenomenon from its
sources. Locate the conceptual gap: what connection/premise/consequence is still unclear?
Choose a next move because of this gap: learn, derive, connect, reframe, or hold. Explain why
that move could change understanding. For learning, use this gap in learning_request.gap and
why_now, and formulate targeted queries; do not request a broad survey merely to fill a stage.
In discussion, take up a peer's concrete relation and explain how your discipline extends,
challenges or changes its consequences. Generic agreement about controls or feasibility is
not a substitute; a measurement contribution is valid when its specific consequences matter.
Study returned services against the gap that requested them, including failures and pending
capabilities. Do not call retrieval success learning. If nothing changes, say so and preserve
the gap. Own previous_steps carry unfinished thinking across phases and sessions. When the
controller flags repeated_no_change, reconsider the missing connection, premise, or next
learning move; holding a branch is valid. The flag uses supplied peer content comparisons, not a quality verdict. A shared interpretation is normal.
Return development_step:{focus:{source:exact development_cycle.sources key,quote:exact excerpt},
gap:nonempty text, action:learn/derive/connect/reframe/hold, reason:nonempty text,
expected_change:text or null for hold,
uptake:[{source:exact source key,quote:exact excerpt or null only for unresolved,
effect:revise/extend/challenge/unchanged/unresolved,reason:how this affects the focus,
consequence:conditional consequence or null when none follows}],
outcome:{kind:relation/implication/clarification/unchanged/uncertain,
statement:what changed or did not, remaining_gap:text or null}}.
Account once for EACH service key in required_service_uptake. If peer_sources is nonempty,
engage at least one (unresolved with a reason is valid). Other uptake is optional. Quotes must
come from the named source; for published claims quote readable source content, not metadata.
For relation/implication outcomes, preserve the resulting claim in a hypothesis_update's
assumption or implications. This records an author's proposal, NOT confirmed novelty/progress.
No compulsory new relation, branch, agreement, data, experiment, proof or implementation.

Use controller-owned question_state, never invent question_before/question_after.
Keep hypotheses tied to specific entities/relations in this situation. A measurement or representation contribution is legitimate; explain its concrete consequences without forcing a natural mechanism.

0","next_offset":12000,"total_characters":36481,"raw_original":false},{"ref":"Dd1578d95ae2cab1ade02","sha256":"d1578d95ae2cab1ade02836ebe214437846c219cfdb4ccfa324d5a3935cf8b4e","pointer":"/text","offset":0,"text":"\"Intelligence embodied in biological cellular architectures often appears to mediate macroscopic dynamic responses to external mechanical stimuli. For example, mechanotransduction of sensitive plants, such as the Venus flytrap ( Aldrovanda vesiculosa ) or  Mimosa pudica L 1 , 2 ., leads to controlled opening and closing of their leaves, as the mechanical outcome of biochemical operations in response to environmental mechanical stimuli. Although seemingly binary, this behavior requires intelligent “computation” involving responsiveness to time-stamped inputs (e.g., two consecutive mechanical stimulations of the same sensory hair) 3 – 5  or sensitivity to intensity 6 , 7 , implying that computational operations between non-electrical signals engage deeply in the formulation of intelligent “living machines”.\\nSimilarly, the design of computational responses in synthetic architected materials, termed “mechanical computing”, is of growing interest in intelligent matter and machines that perform tasks between non-electrical environmental signals, such as soft robots 8 . In this framework, computational operations are executed solely by deformation and transition dynamics of architected materials, thus featuring unconventional, electronics-free information processing with environmental signals being seamlessly coupled. To harness this advantage, ongoing efforts have been directed to supplant conventional components (e.g., gears and linkages) 9  with soft architected materials entailing mechanical information 8 . Specifically, multistable configurations of mechanical elements that leverage snap-through instabilities of soft elastic beams 10 – 17 , shell 18 – 21 , or origami linkages 22 – 24  abstract digitization of mechanical information. When triggered, transition behaviors between buckling modes of structurally coupled mechanical bits lead to a cascade of storage and release of elastic potential energy, which in turn results in localization 16 , 25 , propagation in the form of mechanical transition waves 11 , 13 , 26 , and/or logic operations 11 , 15 , 27 , 28 . Efforts are now growing to employ multiple stimuli and controlling signals (e.g., electronic signals 29 – 32 , magnetic fields 33 – 36 , chemical stimuli 12 , 37 , humidity gradients 22 , fluid pressure 18 , 19 , 38 , 39 , etc.) that provide opportunities for further advancing the embedded processing capability, programmability, and robotic applications.\\nComputational autonomy as a material property per se—that is, information can be transmitted, processed, and retained solely through soft material configurations in the absence of external power sources— is the primary advantage of mechanical computing 8 , 15 , 28 . As mechanical mechanisms encoded in material configurations account for a larger proportion in information processing, a more advanced form of completely mechanical computation (i.e., autonomous operation without any external powering or active elements) becomes critical. However, the exclusion of active elements in intelligent matter design has largely been overlooked. Indeed, demonstrations of purely mechanical computing processes have so far been limited to single logic gates and the corresponding fundamental logical functions 12 , 15 , 22 , 27 , 28 . Although it is quite well established by conventional integrated circuits (ICs) that the computation capability is generally proportionate to the number of computing units, currently, no studies have provided meaningful insight to the design solution for computational autonomy in soft matter consisting of multiple mechanical computing units (termed “mechanologics”) intertwined with each other 22 . Central to this challenge is the dissipation-free transmission of computational mechanical information through a network of mechanologic clusters without the aid of external intervention or powering. A systematic understanding of mechanical signals that propagate through structurally heterogeneous mechanologics is lacking, despite both propagation in homogeneous media 11 , 35 , 40  and operation within stand-alone mechanologics 12 , 22 , 27 , 28  being relatively well studied. Accumulation of potential energy barrier (or mechanical impedance) from cascaded mechanologics acting against the propagating signals also remains an intractable problem.\\nHere, we present a design framework for computational mechanical metamaterials that enable multi-level cascaded logic computation of propagating mechanical signals. Taking inspiration from a mature design paradigm of electronic system architectures (Supplementary Fig.  1 ), we demonstrate how the systematic assembly of soft bistable unit elements leads to a monolithic, integrated computing architecture consisting of a network of mechanologics connected via transmission lines (Fig.  1a ). In this architecture, digital information is transmitted in the form of non-dispersive mechanical solitary waves, and its computation is performed by the dynamic mechanical coupling of the solitary waves with structural heterogeneity in mechanical computing units. Two characteristic energy terms, the input energy barrier ( U b ) and the output transmissive energy ( U out ), are introduced to develop a simplified model of solitary wave-based mechanical computation (Fig.  1b ). Based on the model, we show that the soliton width,  W soliton , is the critical factor governing the behavior of both signal transmission and computation, and explore how to design transmission lines and mechanologics through which mechanical information performs dissipation-free cascaded computing without the use of any active elements (Fig.  1c, d ). These findings allow us to generalize a design rule for implementing system-level integrated mechanical computing. ","next_offset":24000,"total_characters":36481,"raw_original":false},{"ref":"D335384754eedae137eac","sha256":"335384754eedae137eac6d84521b2c149dd6950396a0b70e5a66bca113da3f4a","pointer":"/text","offset":0,"text":"\"Intelligence embodied in biological cellular architectures often appears to mediate macroscopic dynamic responses to external mechanical stimuli. For example, mechanotransduction of sensitive plants, such as the Venus flytrap ( Aldrovanda vesiculosa ) or  Mimosa pudica L 1 , 2 ., leads to controlled opening and closing of their leaves, as the mechanical outcome of biochemical operations in response to environmental mechanical stimuli. Although seemingly binary, this behavior requires intelligent “computation” involving responsiveness to time-stamped inputs (e.g., two consecutive mechanical stimulations of the same sensory hair) 3 – 5  or sensitivity to intensity 6 , 7 , implying that computational operations between non-electrical signals engage deeply in the formulation of intelligent “living machines”.\\nSimilarly, the design of computational responses in synthetic architected materials, termed “mechanical computing”, is of growing interest in intelligent matter and machines that perform tasks between non-electrical environmental signals, such as soft robots 8 . In this framework, computational operations are executed solely by deformation and transition dynamics of architected materials, thus featuring unconventional, electronics-free information processing with environmental signals being seamlessly coupled. To harness this advantage, ongoing efforts have been directed to supplant conventional components (e.g., gears and linkages) 9  with soft architected materials entailing mechanical information 8 . Specifically, multistable configurations of mechanical elements that leverage snap-through instabilities of soft elastic beams 10 – 17 , shell 18 – 21 , or origami linkages 22 – 24  abstract digitization of mechanical information. When triggered, transition behaviors between buckling modes of structurally coupled mechanical bits lead to a cascade of storage and release of elastic potential energy, which in turn results in localization 16 , 25 , propagation in the form of mechanical transition waves 11 , 13 , 26 , and/or logic operations 11 , 15 , 27 , 28 . Efforts are now growing to employ multiple stimuli and controlling signals (e.g., electronic signals 29 – 32 , magnetic fields 33 – 36 , chemical stimuli 12 , 37 , humidity gradients 22 , fluid pressure 18 , 19 , 38 , 39 , etc.) that provide opportunities for further advancing the embedded processing capability, programmability, and robotic applications.\\nComputational autonomy as a material property per se—that is, information can be transmitted, processed, and retained solely through soft material configurations in the absence of external power sources— is the primary advantage of mechanical computing 8 , 15 , 28 . As mechanical mechanisms encoded in material configurations account for a larger proportion in information processing, a more advanced form of completely mechanical computation (i.e., autonomous operation without any external powering or active elements) becomes critical. However, the exclusion of active elements in intelligent matter design has largely been overlooked. Indeed, demonstrations of purely mechanical computing processes have so far been limited to single logic gates and the corresponding fundamental logical functions 12 , 15 , 22 , 27 , 28 . Although it is quite well established by conventional integrated circuits (ICs) that the computation capability is generally proportionate to the number of computing units, currently, no studies have provided meaningful insight to the design solution for computational autonomy in soft matter consisting of multiple mechanical computing units (termed “mechanologics”) intertwined with each other 22 . Central to this challenge is the dissipation-free transmission of computational mechanical information through a network of mechanologic clusters without the aid of external intervention or powering. A systematic understanding of mechanical signals that propagate through structurally heterogeneous mechanologics is lacking, despite both propagation in homogeneous media 11 , 35 , 40  and operation within stand-alone mechanologics 12 , 22 , 27 , 28  being relatively well studied. Accumulation of potential energy barrier (or mechanical impedance) from cascaded mechanologics acting against the propagating signals also remains an intractable problem.\\nHere, we present a design framework for computational mechanical metamaterials that enable multi-level cascaded logic computation of propagating mechanical signals. Taking inspiration from a mature design paradigm of electronic system architectures (Supplementary Fig.  1 ), we demonstrate how the systematic assembly of soft bistable unit elements leads to a monolithic, integrated computing architecture consisting of a network of mechanologics connected via transmission lines (Fig.  1a ). In this architecture, digital information is transmitted in the form of non-dispersive mechanical solitary waves, and its computation is performed by the dynamic mechanical coupling of the solitary waves with structural heterogeneity in mechanical computing units. Two characteristic energy terms, the input energy barrier ( U b ) and the output transmissive energy ( U out ), are introduced to develop a simplified model of solitary wave-based mechanical computation (Fig.  1b ). Both are history-dependent hysteresis models that are used to model magnetic hysteresis. Memory index: available_index {} and retrieved [] — so no pre-existing long-term notes for me. I must build my own understanding and return 0-3 memory notes.

Now the case: hysteron. Data: calibration (spring force-length), threshold measurements (pair_A: rotor 1 and 2, up/down, other_state ±1, mount_l varying 0-4.731 cm), pair_B: crossed coupling, only mount_l=4.7, 8 threshold rows; network_C: 16 state events in cyclic driving with 4 rotors.

I'm the domain scientist in 弹性机构、刚体力学与准静态实验 (elastic mechanisms, rigid body mechanics, quasistatic experiments). My independent contribution should be a mechanics-based understanding: given geometry (rotor bars, pivots spaced w, driving spring attached at L, coupling springs at ell), derive the potential energy landscape and switching thresholds as function of gamma, and hysteron definitions (up/down threshold pairs), and how a coupling interaction shifts the thresholds of one rotor conditioned on the other's state — the "hysteron" concept in Preisach sense requires each element to have a fixed up/down threshold pair independent of others' states; but here the interaction makes thresholds depend on other_state → this is the key tension: whether the two-rotor device can be described as two independent hysterons or requires "interaction" (a hysteron pair with state-dependent thresholds). Actually the threshold table gives exactly both: threshold of rotor 1 up with other_state = -1 vs +1. Compare: at mount_l 0 and 1.577, thresholds equal (7.3, 7.1 in both) — interaction vanishes when coupling attachment at pivot (ell=0 → no torque amplification). At 3.154 and 4.731, they differ (6.5 vs 5.9; 5.5 vs 4.3). Interesting: interaction grows with ell (moment arm). That is a clean mechanics story: interaction torque ∝ ell, so threshold shift ∝ ell·sin(θ)/... The "state-dependence" of thresholds = Preisach-violating interaction, and the data quantifies its onset. At ell=0 interaction exactly zero → threshold exactly independent of other state (verified in up 7.3=7.3, 7.1=7.1; down -7.1=-7.1 for rotor1 up? rows 76,80 both -7.1).

Actually a nice worked calculation: estimate the interaction-induced threshold shift Δγ(ell) and test whether it scales linearly with ell (moment arm) — can be computed from threshold table. And check up-down asymmetry. Also for pair_B (crossed springs, ell=4.7): shifts huge (rotor2 up 24.9 vs 30.7; rotor1 down -1.5 vs 9.7 — sign change!). This crossed configuration makes interaction strong and sign-flipping.

Then network_C: 16 events, single flips each, cyclic repeat exactly (events 1-8 repeated at 9-16). Event data at fixed threshold rankings. The domain scientist's angle: rigid-body/quasistatic mechanics — the effective potential energy U(θ1,θ2;γ) = sum of driving-spring energy + coupling spring energies; equilibria and saddle-node bifurcations give the up/down thresholds; interaction energy term leads to a shift that is asymmetric for parallel vs crossed spring pairs (sign of ∂²U/∂θ1∂θ2). A "hysteron" only exists for each rotor when the other's switching is much slower/faster? Actually the concept: "hysteron generation" — how a single rotor plus coupling produces hysterons, and how networks generate multi-hysteron transition graphs.

Key conceptual tension I can develop: Preisach-style superposition assumes each hysteron's up/down thresholds (α, β) are fixed numbers, so the state of the network is determined by the sequence of past drive extrema (wiping-out, congruency). Here interactions mean the effective thresholds depend on neighbours' states: α_i(s_j). Then the transition graph can become "non-Preischach": shear in the (γ_i) thresholds; e.g., in network_C, events at fixed drive values (4.5, 5.8, 5.8, -3.3...) with single flips — meaning the network behaves like an ordered set of independent hysterons with well-separated thresholds — the observed absence of avalanches (all 16 events single flips) can be read as evidence that interaction shifts are smaller than the gaps between thresholds (a "weak-interaction / no-avalanche" regime). That's a testable conditional consequence: avalanche requires |Δ_threshold from neighbour| > threshold gap. And pair_A gives the sizes of interaction shift (≈ up to 1.2 cm) whereas in network_C the drive-level spacings at up-events 4.5, 5.8, 5.8, 5.9 differ by ~0.1-1.3 cm — interesting: at pair level the shift from interaction is comparable to the gaps in network_C. So conditional: either network_C's couplings are much weaker/shorter moment arms, or the two coincident events at 5.8 are a cascade disguised as sequential events (two rotors flipping at same drive value: events 2 (s1 flips) and 3 (s3 flips) both at 5.8; and 6,7 both at -5.1). Since events at identical drive values can't distinguish driving-order vs interaction-triggered, the recorded data cannot tell whether the second flip at the same γ was driven directly by the rod or triggered by neighbour flip — a genuinely undetermined observation, and a good topic for asking peer/case definition.

Wait, more careful: event 2 changes s1 (-+-+ → ++-+) at 5.8, event 3 changes s3 (++-+ → ++++) also at 5.8. So at γ=5.8, both rotors 1 and 3 flipped. Were these simultaneous or sequential? order recorded. That's an ambiguity.

Also: geometric/energetic constraint I can derive as a worked calculation: the coupling spring length as function of (θ1, θ2): ell_i sinθ... Let's consider each rotor: a rigid bar pivoted at its center? "Rigid bars rotate freely about central pivots" — theta=0 points along y. Pivots spaced w=15.2 cm apart horizontally. Coupling spring attachment at distance ell from pivot: point = (±ell sin? ...). Mounting coordinates x_mount_offsets. Coupling spring connects attachment points of the two rotors, with rest length. Energy = ½k(ℓ_s − ℓ_0)². The interaction torque on rotor 1 = ∂U_c/∂θ1 = k(ℓ_s−ℓ_0)·(∂ℓ_s/∂θ1). Since ∂ℓ_s/∂θ1 ∝ ell, threshold shift ∝ ell·(something)·cos... This gives Δγ ∝ ell approximately for small ell — matching data roughly? Let's check pair_A rotor1 up: other=-1 vs +1: Δ = 0, 0, -0.6, -1.2 for ell=0,1.577,3.154,4.731. Roughly linear in ell beyond 1.577 (slope ~ -0.00038/cm per cm? from 3.154→4.731 (Δell=1.577), Δshift = -0.6 → -0.38 per cm; from 1.577→3.154, -0.6 → -0.38/cm. And 0→1.577: 0 though. Hmm — nonzero rest length 2.4-2.6 cm and mounting offsets mean at ell=1.577 attachments may be far from the spring's compression/tension transition; maybe the force sign flips. Fine: linear scaling with moment arm × coupling force, and sign determined by whether the coupling spring is in tension or compression in that configuration. That's a defensible mechanics reading: Δthreshold ∝ ell × (axial force in coupling spring), so zero shift can occur when spring force ≈ rest (zero-tension point) — not necessarily at ell=0 only. Good insight: the shift's dependence on the other state can be understood as a "pre-stress/axial-force lever": the coupling spring produces torque = ℓ × F_component; changing the neighbour's state changes spring length (and hence axial force) hence changing torque per unit ℓ.

Let me also compute: rigid-body torque balance for a single rotor: driving spring attached at L, rest lengths given, pivot geometry: driving spring from attachment point to horizontal rod at height y=9.4? Torque balance: k_d(ℓ_d(θ)−ℓ_0)·L·cos... + coupling torque + stop torque = 0. Threshold is saddle-node where dτ/dθ = 0 (marginal stability). That gives a quantitative framework for the "hysteron" origin: hysteresis arises from non-monotonicity of the torque–angle relation (geometric nonlinearity of spring attachment: the spring's moment arm L sinθ decreasing past θ=0 plus the stop). Actually with a single attached linear spring, the restoring torque is k(L sinθ ... )... Let me think precisely.

Coordinates: pivot at origin, bar of length? theta measured from y-axis (θ=0 along y). Attachment point at distance L along the bar: (L sinθ, L cosθ) if θ measured from +y toward +x. The drive rod translates horizontally at some fixed vertical height y_c (y=9.4 cm per apparatus? that's "y_cm": 9.4). The driving spring connects the attachment point to a point on the translating rod: rod point at (γ, y). So spring vector = (γ − L sinθ, y − L cosθ), length ℓ_d. Force magnitude F_d = k_d(ℓ_d − ℓ_0) (tension positive). Torque about pivot from spring force on the bar = r × F where F = −k(ℓ_d−ℓ_0)·(r_spring/ℓ_d) pointing from bar point toward rod point... Actually force on bar = k(ℓ_d−ℓ_0) * unit vector pointing from bar attach point toward rod attach point (if tension pulls toward rod). r = L(sinθ, cosθ). τ = r_x F_y − r_y F_x = L[(sinθ)F_y − cosθ F_x].

So τ_drive(θ;γ) = k(ℓ_d−ℓ_0)/ℓ_d · L[ sinθ(y − L cosθ) − cosθ(γ − L sinθ) ] = k(ℓ−ℓ_0)/ℓ · L[ y sinθ − γ cosθ ].

The bracket y sinθ − γ cosθ = R sin(θ − φ) with R = sqrt(y²+γ²), φ = atan2(γ, y). Nice: the torque vanishes when tanθ = γ/y, i.e. θ = φ — the bar aligns with the line from pivot to rod point. Meanwhile ℓ_d = |(γ − L sinθ, y − L cosθ)| and ℓ_d² = γ²+y²+L² − 2L(γ sinθ + y cosθ) = R² + L² − 2LR cos(θ − φ). So ℓ_d = sqrt(R²+L²−2LR cos(θ−φ)) — law of cosines! That's neat: the spring energy U = ½k(ℓ_d − ℓ_0)², and ∂U/∂θ = ... = k(ℓ_d−ℓ_0)·(−∂ℓ_d/∂θ)... Let's compute ∂ℓ_d/∂θ = LR sin(θ−φ)/ℓ_d. So torque τ = −∂U/∂θ = −k(ℓ_d−ℓ_0)·LR sin(θ−φ)/ℓ_d. Which matches formula above (sign conventions). So the driving torque is k(ℓ−ℓ_0)/ℓ · LR sin(θ−φ) — a beautifully compact relation: it vanishes at alignment θ=φ (zero moment arm) and switches sign there.

That's an important mechanical insight for the explanation: the driving spring alone gives a torque that is a "sine of misalignment" times (ℓ−ℓ_0)/ℓ; the equilibrium condition τ_total=0. Hysteresis and bistability need non-monotonicity; but with hard stops, the "states" are the stops! Indeed: "Rigid bars rotate freely about central pivots between hard angular stops" — so the two "states" ±1 are the two hard stops. Then the switch happens when the quasistatic torque balance at the stop becomes unstable: the rotor leaves stop when the net torque about pivot (drive + coupling) directed away from the stop exceeds zero. That is a *statics* condition, not a snap-through of a bistable potential — the hysteron arises from the hard stops + geometry (moment arm reversal), i.e., the up-threshold and down-threshold differ because at each stop the torque arm and spring length differ. That's a substantial, concrete insight in my discipline: this device's hysteresis is "stops + geometric moment-arm", not a double-well elastic potential. So each rotor is a hysteron whose (α, β) come from static torque balance at each stop with geometric asymmetry.

Then, with this, up-threshold for rotor 1 at other_state=-1: γ ≈ 7.3; down threshold γ ≈ −7.1 → nearly symmetric. Rotor 2: up 3.5, down 0.1 → strongly asymmetric (bias). Stops angles asymmetric for rotor 2: [-9.8, 11.2] degrees (smaller range) vs rotor 1 [-36.6, 36.7]. And x_mount_offsets [0, -1.9] shift rotor 2's pivot relative to drive rod → geometric bias. Nice: a pivot offset by 1.9 cm relativizes γ → effective γ_eff = γ − x_offset; up/down thresholds for rotor 2 at 3.5 and 0.1: midpoint 1.8 ≈ offset 1.9! Very nice: rotor 2's bias comes from the mount offset. Check rotor1 offset 0: up 7.3, down −7.1: midpoint 0.1 ≈ 0. 

So a clean conditional derivation: for a hysteron made of a bar-on-stops with a linear spring drive, the up/down threshold midpoint equals the geometric pivot offset (zero-moment-arm alignment), and the half-width equals the misalignment needed to overcome... something: half-width 7.2 for rotor1 (L=6.3, y=9.4, stops ±36.6°) and for rotor2 half-width (3.5−0.1)/2 = 1.7. Stops ±9.8/11.2 and offsets. Let's test with formula: at a stop θ_s, torque balance: k(ℓ−ℓ_0)/ℓ · LR sin(θ_s−φ) + τ_coupling = 0 (if free stop has no reaction). Removal of the weight makes the scale return to its initial position. Reversibility is an essential feature for this device to function. Now, assume that instead of the kitchen scale you use a sandbag. A weight placed on the sandbag will compress its surface in proportion to it; however, the sandbag lacks the feature of reversibility. Not only will removal of the weight fail to cause a reversion of the bag to its initial shape, but subsequent weights put on the bag will change the current deformation state little, unless you place a heavier weight on it. However, the sandbag does measure something: the largest deformation it has been subjected to in its past. Thus, while the kitchen scale measures a state, the shape of the sandbag provides information about its deformation history. It is a conceptually simple example for memory formation in matter ( 1 ) and demonstrates that the disorder of the grains, as well as the dissipation of energy when the sandbag is deformed, play an essential role in its irreversible behavior. On the other hand, it is precisely this irreversibility which permits one to go from measuring states to measuring histories and thereby encoding memory. In PNAS, Shohat et al. ( 2 ) investigate memory formation in crumpled sheets of paper. Exploring the complex interplay of the geometry and mechanics of wrinkled paper, they demonstrate how memory emerges from the interactions of bistable mechanical instabilities formed by its folds and creases. The findings of Shohat et al. ( 2 ) are remarkable, since they demonstrate in an explicit and experimentally accessible manner how memory can emerge in everyday systems such as a crumpled sheet of paper, thereby contributing toward our understanding of memory formation in driven disordered systems.\\nMemory-recording mechanical devices can be constructed from bistable elements ( 3 ) such as origami bellows ( 4 ), corrugated elastic sheets ( 5 ), and, more generally, mechanical metamaterials ( 6 ). Under a compression, a bistable element remains in one of its stable states, call it “0,” until the force rises above a threshold level  F + , upon which a fast relaxation snap event causes a transition into the other state, “1,” as shown in  Fig. 1  A ,  Top Left . Subsequently reducing the forcing, a transition back into state “0” will occur when the force falls below a threshold level  F − . Hysteresis emerges when the two switching fields  F ±  are such that  F − < F + , so that for values between these two thresholds the actual state of the bistable element depends on the history of the forcing. Such elementary units of hysteresis are called Preisach hysterons ( 7 – 9 ).\\n( A ,  Top Left ) Elementary hysteresis cycle of a Preisach hysteron resulting from a bistable mechanical element with states 0 and 1 under force  F . The hysteron can be in state 1 for  F > F −  and state 0 for  F < F + . In the interval  F − < F < F +  the state depends on the history of the forcing. ( A ,  Center ) The state transition graph of four hysterons each coupling independently to the driving  F . ( A ,  Lower Right ) The ordering of the switching fields  F i ±  is as indicated. Black/gray (red/orange) arrows indicate state changes of the corresponding hysteron  i  when  F  is just above (below)  F i +  ( F i + ). A possible trajectory from 0000 to the state 0101 is shown by the black and red arrows. ( B ,  Top Left ) The experimental set up of ref.  2  for a crumpled sheet of paper driven by a variable strain Δ. ( B ,  Center ) The force–strain response under cyclic straining, once a periodic cycle has set in (yellow cycle). A subsequent driving protocol of the form shown in the lower right inset results in the subcycles shown. Adapted from Shohat et al. ( 2 ). The transition graph ( A ) and the cyclically sheared paper response ( B ) reveal a hierarchy of nested cycles characteristic of RPM.\\nConsider now a collection of  N  hysterons, each with a pair of threshold forces  F i ± , and each coupling independently to the applied force  F . One can construct a history-recording device by ordering the threshold forces as  F 1 + < F 2 + < … < F N +  and  F 1 − > F 2 − > … > F N − , as sketched in  Fig. 1 A ,  Lower Right . Initializing the device in a configuration where each hysteron is in its “0” state, upon increasing the force they will change states one by one in the order  1 , 2 , … , N . Due to the choice of ordering the  F i − , this will be also the same order in which the elements return from their “1” to their “0” state. A state transition graph of this system for the case  N  = 4 is shown in  Fig. 1 A . Here, gray/black (orange/red) arrows indicate transitions when the force has just increased (decreased) enough so that one element becomes unstable and changes state.\\nNote the nesting of cycles in  Fig. 1 A :  Starting from the state 0010, a sequence of gray/black arrows followed by orange/red arrows leads via 1110 back to 0010, forming a graph cycle, which in turn is nested within the cycle between states 0000 and 1110, etc. Observe also that from any state in the graph, by lowering the forcing sufficiently we can “reset” the system by bringing it back to the state 0000. The hierarchical nesting of cycles within cycles is a characteristic feature associated with return-point memory (RPM) ( 10 ), which emerges in the hysteretical magnetization response of magnets to an applied magnetic field. In the transition graph setting, the nesting feature is a topological property of the transitions between hysteron states, which is referred to as loop RPM ( 11 ). Assume now that starting in state 0000 a sequence of forcings leads the system to state 0101. The hierarchical nesting of cycles constrains the possible trajectories that the system must have followed in order to reach 0101 from the zero state: In particular, in the recent past the force must have risen above the value of  F 3 + , subsequently fallen, but not below  F 3 − , then risen again to a value between  F 2 +  and  F 3 + , etc. The shortest trajectory from 0000 to 0101 has been highlighted by the red and black arrows in  Fig. 1 A .\\nRemarkably, mechanical instabilities, which give rise to hysteresis in the form of near-perfect RPM with a hierarchy of nested hysteresis cycles, are rather ubiquitous. They are found in the athermal quasi-static response of various driven disordered systems, such as simulations of amorphous solids under shear strain ( 12 ) and experiments on sheared colloidal suspensions ( 13 ) as well as jammed granular particles under uniaxial compression ( 14 ). In all these systems thermal effects are negligible, and the mechanical instabilities are due to spatially localized plastic events, called soft spots ( 15 – 17 ), which effectively respond as hysterons. However, in contrast to the collection of noninteracting Preisach hysterons, these soft spots interact with each other via long-range elastic deformations. As a result, the state change of one soft spot can alter the switching fields of the other, but it can also give rise to new soft spots or deactivate existing ones by disabling their switching behavior. Overall, these interactions can give rise to highly complex dynamics, including avalanches where the instability of one soft spot triggers instabilities of multiple others, and more generally dynamically critical phenomena, such as yielding. The Preisach model, due to the absence of interactions, lacks all this complexity. Nevertheless, it is a conceptually simple model to illustrate key mechanisms of memory formation, such as RPM, serving a role similar to the ideal gas in statistical mechanics.\\nThe interactions between hysterons turn out to be both a blessing and a curse. They are a curse since in principle interactions can destroy the hierarchical RPM-type nesting of hysteresis cycles and hence adversely affect the capability of memory formation. They are a blessing since the interactions permit a degree of “programmability”: Cyclically driving the system until a periodic response has set in is tantamount to selecting a set of interacting soft spots that “play nice” with each other, i.e., they only moderately influence or impede each other’s switching behavior so that an RPM-like hierarchy of nested cycles remains largely intact.\\nSurprisingly, many of the driven disordered systems mentioned above achieve both the programmability and nesting of hysteresis cycles, and the reasons for this are still not sufficiently understood. Now the paper by Shohat et al. ( 2 ) adds one more such system to the fray: a thin sheet of crumpled paper subject to driving via stretching and unstretching it ( Fig. 1 B ). The relation between the complex geometry of folds and creases of a crumpled sheet of paper and its mechanical response to external driving has so far been largely unexplored. By combining cyclic stretching protocols with three-dimensional (3D) imaging, Shohat et al. ( 2 ) are able to correlate the mechanical response of the sheet to its local geometrical transformation.\\nShohat et al. ( 2 ) find that when the sheet is cyclically strained it settles into a near-perfect periodic force–strain hysteresis cycle dotted with a large number of abrupt force jumps. Using 3D imaging, Shohat et al. ( 2 ) are able to trace the force jumps to localized plastic events in the sheet, originating from the snapping of vertices formed by the crossings of ridges ( 18 ). Shohat et al. ( 2 ) demonstrate that these mechanical instabilities behave as hysterons that interact with each other. As in the sheared amorphous solids, depending on the locations and states of the other hysterons, the interactions can facilitate or impede each other’s switching behavior. The sheet of paper has become a mechanical realization of a spin glass, an archetypical model for understanding the emergence of complexity in disordered systems ( 19 ).\\nThese findings set the stage for a thorough investigation of memory formation. First, Shohat et al. ( 2 ) “program” their sheet of paper by applying cyclic strain over a strain range  [ Δ 0 min , Δ 0 max ]  until a periodic response is attained in the force–strain response of the sheet ( Fig. 1 B ). The response to cyclic deformation has all the hallmarks of RPM. Once a periodic response has set in, a subsequent reduction of  Δ 0 max  to  Δ 1 max  results in force-versus-strain subcycles of the original hysteresis cycle, as depicted in  Fig. 1 B . In fact, the amplitude  Δ 1 max  can be lowered and raised as long as  Δ 1 max ≤ Δ 0 max , i.e., it does not exceed the value at which the original hysteresis cycle was obtained. Raising  Δ 1 max  back to  Δ 0 max , the original cycle is recovered. Thus, applying oscillatory shear to the crumpled paper has led to the selection of an interacting hysteron system that supports a hierarchy of cycles and subcycles, as shown in  Fig. 1 B . As in simulations of sheared amorphous solids ( 12 ), the emergence of the interacting hysteron system is at the heart of the memory that is imprinted into the disordered system as a result of cyclic loading. In fact, raising  Δ 1 max  to a value above  Δ 0 max  and then back to  Δ 0 max , Shohat et al. ( 2 ) show that this memory is erased.\\nThe relative ease with which the interacting hysterons of a driven disordered system establish a hierarchy of nested hysteresis cycles suggests that this may not have to be a consequence of the cyclic driving. The approximate rate independence of the response implies that the duration of the driving cycle is not important, while the hierarchy of nested cycles suggests that the driving need not be periodic, as long as it is confined to some range, e.g., the interval  [ Δ 0 min , Δ 0 max ]  in the case of the crumpled sheet. {"result": {"summary": "从弹性机构/刚体静力学的独立初读：本案例的“态”不是双阱势的两个阱，而是刚性杆顶在硬停位上的两种接触状态；因此单转子阈值不是逃逸势垒，而是一个纯几何对齐条件。把驱动杆读成一个可旋转的“有效重力方向”后可得 γ_th = y·tanθ_stop − x_i（y=9.4 cm，x_i 为驱动弹簧在杆上的安装偏移），用它预测 pair_A 在 ell=0 的四条阈值误差仅 0.0–0.3 cm，环宽 2y·tanθ 也几乎命中（14.0 vs 14.4；3.48 vs 3.4）。这解释了 x_mount_offsets=[0,−1.9] 为何恰好给出转子2 的中点偏置 1.8 cm。", "interpretation": "（1）装置读法：转子=受停位约束的摆，驱动弹簧力矩 ∝ k(ℓ−ℓ0)·L·R·sin(θ−φ)/ℓ，R=√(y²+γ_eff²)、φ=atan(γ_eff/y)；力矩过零于“杆与驱动点共线”，故阈值由停位角与安装偏移唯一决定，与 k、静长无关（弱耦合极限）。把这一读法作为学习性示例与实测核对成立（pair_A 全部四条、pair_B 转子1 中点）。
（2）阈值表的结构：40 条阈值行支持一个很干净的分解——邻态只整体平移阈值对，不改环宽。逐 ell 核对：转子1 的 up 与 down 随 other_state 同向平移 0/0.1/0.6/1.2 cm（两者之差 ≤0.1 cm），转子2 为 0/0.4/1.9/4.4 cm；而同一 ell 下两种 other_state 的环宽几乎相同（转子1：14.4/14.4、13.6/13.8、12.0/12.0、9.2/9.2；转子2：3.4/3.4、3.2/3.2、2.8/3.0、2.2/2.2）。pair_B（交叉耦合、k=0.19）同样：转子1 up 6.7↔17.7（Δ=11.0）与 down −1.5↔9.7（Δ=11.2），转子2 Δ=5.8/5.2。故可写 α_i(s)=α_i0(ell)+K_i(ell)s_邻、β_i(s)=β_i0(ell)+K_i(ell)s_邻，环宽 W_i(ell) 与 s_邻 无关。K 的符号在平行耦合为负、交叉耦合为正（−0.6/−2.2 vs +5.6/+2.8 cm per unit s），证实耦合几何可翻号。这里顺带纠正上一阶段材料记录 M3 的一处前提：转子1 并非“不随 other_state 变号”，而是 up 与 down 成对同向平移，差别只在幅度（0.6 vs 2.2）。

Excellent. The materials records (from previous stage, not my own hypothesis) include M2, M3, M7, M8. Note M3's observation: "转子1 在两种 other_state 下都下降... 不随状态变号" — hmm, this record says rotor 1 doesn't change sign with other_state. My reading found both thresholds shift uniformly by +1.2 (a field shift, not a width change). Their framing: "expectation: other_state reversal should reverse the shift sign; rotor 1 doesn't comply" — but that's a misreading: they compared the *shift of each threshold separately* rather than as a paired translation. The sign issue: rotor1 up shifts down (7.3→5.5 with other=−1) while down threshold shifts... −7.1→−3.7 (−3.7 is less negative, i.e. increased). So the two thresholds move in opposite *numeric* directions? Wait let's recompute: at ell=4.731, rotor1: other=−1: up 5.5, down −3.7; other=+1: up 4.3, down −4.9. So going from other=−1 to other=+1, up decreases 5.5→4.3 (−1.2) while down goes −3.7→−4.9 (also −1.2). Both move in the same direction (−1.2)! I earlier computed Δ = θ(−1) − θ(+1) = +1.2 for both. So yes: uniform translation. So the M3 claim "rotor1 doesn't change sign with other_state" is a misreading of the raw table (they looked at the fact that up decreased for both other_states as ell increases, which is a separate fact about ell dependence). This is a concrete error in a premise I can correct — good peer/domain contribution: "阈值对整体平移（field shift），而非宽度改变；转子1 的 up 与 down 在 same ell 下随 other_state 同步平移 +1.2 cm，与转子2 一致；M3 所述'转子1 不随状态变号'是把 ell 依赖与 other_state 依赖混在一起读。"

Let me carefully verify rotor1 at ell=3.154: other −1: up 6.5, down −5.5; other +1: up 5.9, down −6.1. Translation: up Δ=+0.6, down Δ=+0.6 ✓. At ell=1.577: up 7.1/7.1 → Δ=0; down −6.5/−6.7 → Δ=+0.2 (within rounding 0.2; hmm 0.2 discrepancy; ±0.1 each so up could be ±0.2). Fine.

Rotor2 ell=3.154: other −1: up 3.9, down 1.1; other +1: up 2.1, down −0.9. Δup=1.8, Δdown=2.0 ✓.

pair_B: r1: up 6.7/17.7 Δ=11.0; down −1.5/9.7 Δ=11.2 ✓. r2: up 24.9/30.7 Δ=5.8; down 2.1/7.3 Δ=5.2 ✓.

So: consistent translation. Widths preserved. This is a solid, checkable empirical structure I can call "刚性平移（field-shift）" and it is the central organizing observation for my hypothesis: interaction acts as an additive field on the drive coordinate rather than a change of coercivity.

And the width at ell varies with ell (rotor1 14.4→9.2; rotor2 3.4→2.2), which is the "width shrinks with ell" — an effect independent of other_state. Interesting: both rotors' widths shrink as ell grows. That's the "unconditional" part: the coupling spring, regardless of neighbour state, stiffens/loads the rotor in a way that reduces the loop width (a "spring-loading"/geometric stiffening). Hmm, width shrink for rotor 1 from 14.4 to 9.2 (36% reduction) is large. Since the coupling spring's torque is roughly odd in ... hmm. Whatever the mechanism, it is a width effect independent of s_other, whereas the field effect depends on s_other. Nice decomposition: 

α_i(s) = α_i^0(ell) + J_i(ell) s_other
β_i(s) = β_i^0(ell) + J_i(ell) s_other

with W_i(ell) = α_i^0 − β_i^0 decreasing in ell. That's a clean parametrization: three numbers per (rotor, ell): midpoint m(ell), width W(ell), interaction J(ell). The data: 
rotor1 (pair_A): m = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.9 for other−1; 0.1,0.2,−0.1,−0.3 for +1 → J1 = 0, 0.05, 0.3, 0.6.
rotor2: m(−1) = 1.8, 1.9, 2.5, 3.8; m(+1) = 1.8, 1.5, 0.6, −0.6 → J2 = 0, 0.2, 0.95, 2.2.
W1 = 14.4, 13.6, 12.0, 9.2; W2 = 3.4, 3.2, 2.8, 2.2.

Both J's grow superlinearly with ell; J2 ≈ 3.7 J1. And W shrink is roughly linear in ell (W1: 14.4 −1.1·ell? at 4.731: 9.2 → −5.2/4.731 = −1.1; at 3.154: 12.0 → −2.4/3.154=−0.76; at 1.577: 13.6 → −0.8/1.577 = −0.5. So also superlinear.)

Hmm interesting: J and ΔW both superlinear in ell and both rotor-dependent. Maybe both come from the same coupling-spring energy second derivative. Concretely the coupling energy U_c(θ1,θ2) = Σ_pairs ½k(ℓ_s − ℓ_0)². Expand around operating point: torque on rotor i τ_i^c = −∂U/∂θ_i; the field shift ∝ the *first* derivative change with s_j (cross term), the width change ∝ curvature (∂²U/∂θ_i²) — i.e., the interaction's "cross term" (J) and the "self-stiffening" (ΔW) are both second derivatives of the same coupling potential: J ~ ∂²U_c/∂θ_1∂θ_2 evaluated at the stop, and ΔW ~ ∂²U_c/∂θ_i² (a spring adds stiffness to the rotor, which changes the torque balance and hence the threshold). But careful: with hard stops and a monotone drive torque, adding stiffness changes the effective threshold by changing the alignment; actually stiffness term adds to dτ/dθ, which shifts the marginal condition. Anyway, functionally: the same coupling element contributes both an interaction term J (off-diagonal) and a self-term (diagonal) — like a network with J_ij and J_ii. Then a natural decomposition: threshold shift Δα_i = J_ii + Σ_j J_ij s_j. In pair_A, the ell-dependence at s_other = ... hmm, but J_ii would appear symmetric with ell, which we see as width shrink? The width shrink is not a translation. Fine: I can say formally the coupling contributes two measurable channels: a symmetric "self-loading" channel that changes the loop width, and an antisymmetric "mutual field" channel that translates the loop. That is a nice representation, and the machinery of "moving Preisach model" (loop translation) vs "random-bond broadening" I hypothesized. My search failed to get full text on moving Preisach, so I should be careful: I have only abstract-level reference (organic ferroelectric Preisach) which doesn't state the moving model. So I'll mark that concept as "my own framing based on mechanics, not yet retrieved published support", open question.

Now a second, deeper point for hypothesis development: the geometric threshold formula. Let me be careful about its derivation, since I want to present it as a learning example. 

Geometry: bar pivoted at origin O, angle θ from y-axis. Attachment point P = L(sinθ, cosθ). Rod point Q = (x_i + γ, y). Wait, released fact: mounting position x_i measured on the driving rod, x_i=0 corresponds to no shift at γ=0. So Q = (γ + x_i, y)? Earlier I derived γ_th = y tanθ + 1.9 for x_i = −1.9, i.e., γ_th = y tanθ − x_i. So Q = (γ − x_i, y)? Hmm with x_i=−1.9, γ−x_i = γ+1.9. If Q_x = γ + x_i = γ −1.9, then tanθ alignment gives γ = y tanθ + 1.9. Hmm: alignment is P and Q and O collinear: tanθ = Q_x/Q_y = (γ + x_i)/y → γ = y tanθ − x_i = y tanθ + 1.9 ✓ (with x_i = −1.9). So Q_x = γ + x_i. Good, simple: Q = (γ + x_i, y).

So alignment condition: γ = y tanθ − x_i. Check rotor1 (x=0, θ=36.6°): γ = 9.4 × 0.7427 = 6.98 vs measured 7.3 (5% off). Down: θ=−36.6: −6.98 vs −7.1 (2%). Rotor2 (x=−1.9, stops −9.8/+11.2): up: 9.4 tan(11.2) + 1.9 = 1.861+1.9 = 3.76 vs 3.5; down: 9.4 tan(−9.8)+1.9 = −1.623+1.9 = 0.28 vs 0.1. Width predicted 3.48 vs measured 3.4. 

Great. Also check pair_B? Stops r1 ±18.3 with x=−8.1: γ_up = 9.4 tan18.3 − (−8.1) = 3.11+8.1 = 11.2 vs measured 6.7 (other−1) / 17.7 (other+1). Hmm — 11.2 sits between 6.7 and 17.7; interesting: pair_B's measured thresholds straddle the geometric prediction, consistent with a huge field shift ±5.5 about 11.2! Indeed midpoint of 6.7 and 17.7 = 12.2 ≈ 11.2. And r2 (stops −38.8/+38.8, x=−16.4): γ_up = 9.4 tan38.8 + 16.4 = 7.56+16.4 = 23.9; measured 24.9 and 30.7 → midpoint 27.8, hmm predicted 23.9 vs 27.8. down: −38.8: 9.4 tan(−38.8)+16.4 = −7.56+16.4 = 8.84; measured 2.1 and 7.3 → midpoint 4.7. Predicted width = 15.1 vs measured width 22.8. So pair_B: widths much larger than geometric prediction, meaning the coupling springs substantially widen (stiffen?) or the stop-probing torque balance is modified statically by coupling (unconditional coupling torque adds to torque balance at the stop, so leaving the stop requires the drive to overcome both the coupling and the geometric term — so the width change isn't just "self-stiffening", it's also a constant static load that differs at the two stops).

Right: with coupling, the torque balance at the stop is τ_drive(θ_s;γ) + τ_c(θ_s, θ_other) = 0. Then Δγ = −τ_c/(∂τ_drive/∂γ). And ∂τ_drive/∂γ at threshold: from formula τ_drive = k(ℓ_d−ℓ_0)/ℓ_d · L(y sinθ − γ cosθ)... derivative w.r.t. γ includes both the (ℓ−ℓ_0)/ℓ factor and the explicit −cosθ; near alignment the bracket vanishes so the dominant term is the bracket derivative: ∂/∂γ[y sinθ − γcosθ] = −cosθ, times Lk(ℓ−ℓ_0)/ℓ. So Δγ = τ_c/[Lk(ℓ_d−ℓ_0)/ℓ_d · cosθ_s]. Thus threshold shift = coupling torque / driving torque lever gain — a fixed conversion factor per rotor and stop. Key consequence: shifts for up and down threshold at the *same* rotor are converted with the same factor only if cosθ and (ℓ−ℓ_0)/ℓ are similar at both stops — which, with symmetric stops (±), gives identical conversion → uniform translation. That's exactly the observed pattern! And it explains why asymmetry in stop angles yields asymmetric shifts (rotor 2: J2 larger than J1? Hmm, conversion factor depends on k, L, L_d... L_d(θ_s) differs).

So the mechanism for "pure field shift": because the coupling torque is applied at the stop (where θ is fixed), it enters the threshold condition as a constant torque, and since the two stops are nearly mirror-symmetric (|θ+| ≈ |θ−|) the same conversion factor applies → the whole loop translates. This is a mechanistic explanation, in my discipline (static torque balance at a hard stop; no snap-through involved). Then: loop width changes with ell because the coupling itself contributes a θ-dependent torque at each stop (it depends on θ_i too, and ell enters both attachment geometry), and the "width" as y[tanθ+] − y[tanθ−] gets modified if the effective alignment changes.

Good, this is genuinely a "organizing principle" of the case: **hard-stop + linear-spring device → hysteron thresholds are determined by static torque balance at each stop (alignment condition), not by an elastic double well; interactions enter additively as torque offsets, hence translate the loop instead of reshaping it; loop width and bias can be tuned geometrically via y, stop angles, mounting offset x_i, and coupling attachment ell.** Conditional consequences: (1) thresholds linear in y (testable by changing rod height), (2) midpoint bias = x_i offset exactly, (3) J ∝ ell_i × (coupling torque at stop) — the ratio J_2/J_1 measured 3.7 should track the ratio of conversion factors ; (4) reversal of coupling sign (crossed vs parallel) flips J sign — pair_B: r1 J = +5.55 per unit s? Let's compute sign: pair_A r1: J = +0.6 (i.e., threshold higher when s_other=−1). Define α_i(s_j) = α_i^0 + J_ij s_j: with s_j = −1 giving higher threshold → J_ij = −0.6? Let's define carefully: θ_th(s_other) = θ_th^0 + K s_other. At s=−1: K(−1) = shift +0.6 relative to s=+1... Let's compute with s=+1 as reference: θ(+1) and θ(−1) = θ(+1) + Δ where Δ = 1.2. Then θ = θ0 + K s, θ(−1) − θ(+1) = −2K = 1.2 → K = −0.6. So K_1 = −0.6, K_2 = −2.2 (per unit s_other) at ell=4.731. Sign: negative K means when neighbour is +, threshold is higher — i.e., alignment (s_i = s_j) is favoured? If neighbour is +, it takes higher drive to switch rotor i to +... wait that means the neighbour + *hinders* rotor i going + → favours anti-alignment? Hmm: K<0: θ_th(s_j=+1) > θ_th(s_j=−1). For the up threshold, with s_j=+1 you need MORE drive to go +, so having a + neighbour makes it harder to become + → anti-ferromagnetic-like (favours s_i = −s_j)? Hmm, careful: the up threshold being higher when s_j = +1 means the + state of j stabilizes the − state of i → anti-alignment favoured. Wait no: if s_j=+1 makes it harder for i to switch to +, then i prefers to remain −; so + neighbour repels + → antiferromagnetic. Hmm, but in pair_A parallel coupling springs — geometrically, parallel bars rotating same sense keep spring length constant (no energy) → antiferromagnetic? Let's think: parallel springs connect P1=(ell1 sinθ1 + x1_pivot, ell1 cosθ1...)? Both bars pivot about their own pivots; parallel attachment points... If θ1 = θ2, then both attachment points move identically, spring length = pivot distance + fixed offset → no stretch: zero energy. If θ1 = −θ2, the points separate → energy cost. That's actually "ferromagnetic" in the sense same-signed rotations cost nothing. But "same state" in the σ = ±1 sense corresponds to same rotation direction only if both bars' σ convention is the same orientation. Anyway, observed K<0 = antiferromagnetic in σ-language. And pair_B crossed geometry: r1: θ(6.7 at s2=−1), θ(17.7 at s2=+1): K = (6.7−17.7)/2 = −5.5, same sign as pair_A! Hmm, M4's record claimed the sign effect reverses (pair_B other=+1 makes up larger, pair_A other=+1 makes up smaller: pair_A r2 up: other−1 4.9, other+1 0.5 → K = (4.9−0.5)/2 = +2.2 — opposite sign to r1! Interesting: within pair_A, rotor1 K<0 and rotor2 K<0? Let's recompute r2: θ(other=−1) = 4.9, θ(other=+1)=0.5. K = (θ(−1) − θ(+1))/(−2) = (4.9−0.5)/(−2) = −2.2. Negative. For r1: θ(−1)=5.5, θ(+1)=4.3 → K = (5.5−4.3)/(−2) = −0.6. Negative. So both negative in pair_A. In pair_B: r1 K = (6.7−17.7)/(−2) = +5.5; r2 K = (24.9−30.7)/(−2) = +2.9. So pair_B K>0 (opposite sign to pair_A). Good: M4's claim "sign effect reverses" is correct at the pair level. My K-formulation makes it crisp: parallel → K<0, crossed → K>0, |K| larger in crossed (5.5, 2.9 vs 0.6, 2.2). Hmm magnitude: pair_A r2 2.2 > pair_B r2 2.9? close. Anyway.

So corrected representation: θ_th,i = m_i(ell) + (W_i(ell)/2) σdirness... let me define α_i(s) = α_i0 + K_i s, β_i(s) = β_i0 + K_i s, with W_i = α_i0 − β_i0. Table of (m_i, W_i, K_i) per (device, rotor, ell). This is a compact "hysteron + local field" parametrization, an object of 3 numbers per hysteron.

Now the network question. With the representation α_i(s) = α_i0 + Σ_j K_ij s_j, the state transition graph is that of an "interacting hysteron" model = a "moving/field-shifted Preisach". Key conditional insight: If |K_ij| are small compared to gaps in α_i0 ordering, the trajectory is that of independent hysterons (RPM nesting preserved) and each event is a single flip; if |K_ij| exceeds a gap, then flipping j can immediately flip i at the same drive value → avalanche of size ≥2 (or, if sign positive and large, can even "prevent" a switch = make a hysteron "inactive"). Observed: in network_C, 8 events/cycle, all single flips; two pairs at identical drive values (5.8, −5.1). Under the "field-shift" representation, the two equal-drive pairs are precisely the observable signature of |K_ij| ≈ gap (i.e., marginal coincidence). But we cannot distinguish a genuine near-coincidence of static thresholds from an interaction-triggered pair without knowing either K_ij or the free-rotor thresholds. That's an honest limitation and a good question to the peer.

Also consequences: the measured "clamped" thresholds in pair_A/B must differ from "free" thresholds by a "spring loading" correction: clamping imposes an extra constraint (holds the neighbour at stop → the coupling spring acts with a fixed end, contributing a static torque) whereas free neighbour would move → smaller effective coupling (series compliance). So clamped J is an upper bound on free J? Hmm, when the neighbour is free, the coupling spring's other end can move (rotational compliance), reducing the torque for a given displacement; but also when free rotor sits at its own stop it's equally stiff until it switches. Statically, near a switch the free neighbour is at a stop (also fixed) unless it's mid-travel — but quiescently rotors rest on stops. So clamped vs free may be quite similar except that a free neighbour might switch during the approach, changing the field — the avalanche case.

So the concrete "clamped→free transfer" claim: J_free ≈ J_clamped but the *event order* changes because the field updates dynamically as neighbours flip (J_ij s_j(t)), which is exactly the mechanism generating distinct up/down orders and possible multi-flip coincidences. That is a crisp conditional statement, better than M6/M8's blanket "interaction threatens transferability".

messages.content: {"status":"read","documents":[{"ref":"Dd1578d95ae2cab1ade02","sha256":"d1578d95ae2cab1ade02836ebe214437846c219cfdb4ccfa324d5a3935cf8b4e","pointer":"/title","offset":0,"text":"\"Integrated mechanical computing for autonomous soft machines.\"","next_offset":null,"total_characters":63,"raw_original":true},{"ref":"Dd1578d95ae2cab1ade02","sha256":"d1578d95ae2cab1ade02836ebe214437846c219cfdb4ccfa324d5a3935cf8b4e","pointer":"/text","offset":0,"text":"\"Intelligence embodied in biological cellular architectures often appears to mediate macroscopic dynamic responses to external mechanical stimuli. For example, mechanotransduction of sensitive plants, such as the Venus flytrap ( Aldrovanda vesiculosa ) or  Mimosa pudica L 1 , 2 ., leads to controlled opening and closing of their leaves, as the mechanical outcome of biochemical operations in response to environmental mechanical stimuli. Although seemingly binary, this behavior requires intelligent “computation” involving responsiveness to time-stamped inputs (e.g., two consecutive mechanical stimulations of the same sensory hair) 3 – 5  or sensitivity to intensity 6 , 7 , implying that computational operations between non-electrical signals engage deeply in the formulation of intelligent “living machines”.\\nSimilarly, the design of computational responses in synthetic architected materials, termed “mechanical computing”, is of growing interest in intelligent matter and machines that perform tasks between non-electrical environmental signals, such as soft robots 8 . In this framework, computational operations are executed solely by deformation and transition dynamics of architected materials, thus featuring unconventional, electronics-free information processing with environmental signals being seamlessly coupled. To harness this advantage, ongoing efforts have been directed to supplant conventional components (e.g., gears and linkages) 9  with soft architected materials entailing mechanical information 8 . Specifically, multistable configurations of mechanical elements that leverage snap-through instabilities of soft elastic beams 10 – 17 , shell 18 – 21 , or origami linkages 22 – 24  abstract digitization of mechanical information. When triggered, transition behaviors between buckling modes of structurally coupled mechanical bits lead to a cascade of storage and release of elastic potential energy, which in turn results in localization 16 , 25 , propagation in the form of mechanical transition waves 11 , 13 , 26 , and/or logic operations 11 , 15 , 27 , 28 . Efforts are now growing to employ multiple stimuli and controlling signals (e.g., electronic signals 29 – 32 , magnetic fields 33 – 36 , chemical stimuli 12 , 37 , humidity gradients 22 , fluid pressure 18 , 19 , 38 , 39 , etc.) that provide opportunities for further advancing the embedded processing capability, programmability, and robotic applications.\\nComputational autonomy as a material property per se—that is, information can be transmitted, processed, and retained solely through soft material configurations in the absence of external power sources— is the primary advantage of mechanical computing 8 , 15 , 28 . As mechanical mechanisms encoded in material configurations account for a larger proportion in information processing, a more advanced form of completely mechanical computation (i.e., autonomous operation without any external powering or active elements) becomes critical. However, the sandbag does measure something: the largest deformation it has been subjected to in its past. HYPOTHESIS DEVELOPMENT v3:
Use your disciplinary understanding and screened long-term memory to develop assumptions.
Start from a specific phenomenon, tension, difficulty or missing relation. When you have a
possible explanation or organizing principle, state what you suppose; merely changing a
'whether' question into an affirmative sentence adds no insight. An assumption can be an
explanation, conjectured relation, representation, distinction or method/construction principle.
Explore what conceptual move it makes and, CONDITIONALLY on the assumption, what changes in
our understanding or possible actions. Develop concrete consequences, not promises of impact.
Use these as thinking moves, not a checklist that every early idea must already satisfy.
Before requesting learning, identify a specific missing conceptual connection in the current
assumption, why it matters, and what understanding might change. Return to that same gap after
reading: explain a revised premise, relation or conditional consequence, or retain the gap.
Do not substitute more citations, caveats, controls or formal wording for conceptual development.
Measurement/method contributions remain valid when their concrete intellectual consequences are
articulated. No compulsory mechanism, scientific breakthrough, or progress at each turn.

In peer discussion, engage a specific assumption: elaborate a consequence, expose a hidden
premise, connect a disciplinary concept, propose a distinct explanation, or revise a relation.
Explain the reasoning. You may retain, revise, branch, or park your own line. No forced consensus,
disagreement, novelty claim, completed hypothesis or compulsory new branch each turn.
Evidence strength, proof, available data/tools, implementation and experimental feasibility
are NOT requirements for proposing, retaining or prioritizing a hypothesis. Do not turn
discussion into a feasibility review. Research/analysis requests remain optional resources
for thinking. Correct concrete errors in premises while keeping conditional hypotheses distinct
from established observations; lack of evidence alone is not a refutation.

hypothesis_state.self contains your saved branches; peer_branches belong to their named owners.
Return hypothesis_updates: [] when nothing changed, otherwise full cards:
{key: stable local identifier [A-Za-z0-9_]+, base_version: 0 for new or supplied own version,
assumption: nonempty provisional claim, motivation: specific phenomenon/difficulty/relation,
conceptual_move: string or null if still unclear,
implications: [specific conditional consequences, may be empty],
open_questions: [unresolved conceptual questions, may be empty],
status: developing/parked, reason: why propose/change/park/resume,
influenced_by: [exact ref objects from supplied hypothesis_state],
depends_on: [exact supplied hypothesis refs used as premises; [] if none]}.
Influence is not logical dependence. Declare depends_on only for actual premises; do not invent
links. revision_obligations lists your branches whose declared premises changed or themselves
await review. This does NOT mean the branch is false. For each obligation return
 dependency_responses:[{ref:exact hypothesis_ref,action:revise/reaffirm/park/unresolved,reason}].
Reaffirm/revise requires an updated full card citing current dependency versions; changing only
links is recorded as provenance maintenance, not conceptual progress. Park/unresolved retains
the branch and its warning. Reasoned reaffirmation is valid; do not mechanically follow criticism.
Dependencies not explicitly declared cannot be inferred by this structural checker.
Omitting a branch retains it. To keep an alternative, use a new key and cite the parent ref;
never overwrite a peer's branch. Missing conceptual_move or implications is allowed for an
early assumption. Keep hypothetical consequences explicitly hypothetical, including examples.
Reusable conceptual learning can also be saved through existing memory_notes, kind:hypothesis,
with actual source provenance and same-key revisions. Run-local branches do not replace your
long-term disciplinary memory or its source screening. Do not invent empirical support.

HYPOTHESIS CONTENT CYCLE:
Use development_cycle as a thinking context, not a demand to invent progress. Choose one
specific explanatory relation, construction, distinction or unresolved phenomenon from its
sources. Locate the conceptual gap: what connection/premise/consequence is still unclear?
Choose a next move because of this gap: learn, derive, connect, reframe, or hold. Explain why
that move could change understanding. For learning, use this gap in learning_request.gap and
why_now, and formulate targeted queries; do not request a broad survey merely to fill a stage.
In discussion, take up a peer's concrete relation and explain how your discipline extends,
challenges or changes its consequences. Generic agreement about controls or feasibility is
not a substitute; a measurement contribution is valid when its specific consequences matter.
Study returned services against the gap that requested them, including failures and pending
capabilities. Do not call retrieval success learning. If nothing changes, say so and preserve
the gap. Own previous_steps carry unfinished thinking across phases and sessions. When the
controller flags repeated_no_change, reconsider the missing connection, premise, or next
learning move; holding a branch is valid. The flag uses supplied peer content comparisons, not a quality verdict. A shared interpretation is normal.

Account once for EACH service key in required_service_uptake. If peer_sources is nonempty,

No compulsory new relation, branch, agreement, data, experiment, proof or implementation.
